newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister suggests legal action on Le Pen.
newsitem.headline: French minister suggests legal action on Le Pen.

text.p: A French cabinet minister on Thursday proposed legal action to silence far-right political leader Jean-Marie Le Pen's espousal of racial inequality, and said the law should be strengthened if it was inadequate.

"Can one say with impunity that human beings do not have equal rights and dignity?" Defence Minister Charles Millon said in a broadcast interview. "I want our entire legal and judicial arsenal to be used against these excesses."
"If our current legal and judicial arsenal is inadequate, the parliament must take up this matter," Millon told RTL radio.

Numerous rights organisations and political leaders, most from the opposition Left, have advocated banning Le Pen's National Front or taking it to court for inciting racial hatred since Le Pen's remarks that racial differences were "a fact".
However, Millon was believed to be the first minister in the centre-right government to do so.
An unrepentant Le Pen said in a television interview on Wednesday, "I don't see why saying one does not believe in racial equality is a violation of human dignity."
"I will not be intimidated by the demonstrations or the threats of a 'thought police'," he told LCI television.
The controversy came amid discussion of election law reforms expected to help the Front break into the National Assembly, where it now has no seats, in the 1998 general elections.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe had last week proposed a reform in election law that political analysts said would enable the Front to win a sizeable bloc of seats in the National Assembly.

A major goal of the reforms appeared to be an attempt at winning good will from Le Pen, who has routinely opposed all the ruling centre-right's candidates, even when a Front candidate was not in the race.
The centre-right is worried that the anti-immigrant National Front could take enough votes from it in 1998 to hand control of parliament to the Left, which governed until 1993.
Le Pen, whose slogan is "France for the French", won 15 percent of the vote in last year's presidential elections.
